title: Nigeria's Rapid Response Register used machine-learning poverty maps to select 1,163 urban wards for COVID-19 cash transfers
summary: ML poverty maps chose 1,163 poorest urban wards for Nigeria's COVID-19 cash register; 49,000 beneficiary households as of 15 Oct 2021
account: Lacking a social registry for urban areas, Nigeria's National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office built the Rapid Response Register for a government-funded COVID-19 cash transfer. Ward-level poverty maps, produced by applying machine-learning algorithms to satellite imagery with household-survey labels (work by Berkeley and Columbia researchers with World Bank economists), selected 1,163 of the poorest urban wards, population over 20 million. Residents self-registered by USSD after SMS blasts (first wave June 2021), followed by in-person verification. Human Rights Watch records that the program began in January 2021 and the PNAS authors state disbursement began mid-January 2021 (day not given; first day of month used). World Bank monitoring reports 49,000 beneficiary households of the government's COVID-CT as of 15 October 2021 and over 1.75 million registrations by November 2021, against a government target of one million households.
purpose: Geographically target a COVID-19 urban cash transfer to the poorest wards where no social registry existed.
system: Ward-level poverty maps from supervised machine learning (deep learning) on satellite imagery, used for geographic targeting in the Rapid Response Register
developer: Joshua Blumenstock (UC Berkeley) and Isabella Smythe (Columbia University), using wealth estimates by Chi et al. (2021), with World Bank economists Jonathan Lain and Tara Vishwanath, for the Government of Nigeria
deployer: National Social Safety Nets Coordinating Office (NASSCO), Federal Government of Nigeria
taxonomy_note: Closest fit: access to cash for urban poor households previously invisible to the registry. Benefit created or restored chosen because the deployment, the registry-identified beneficiaries and a dated beneficiary count (49,000 beneficiary households of the government's COVID-CT as of 15 October 2021, World Bank ISR) are documented; the count is well below the 1 million target.

ratings.reason: Households in selected wards were beneficiaries of the government's COVID-CT (the PNAS authors say disbursement began mid-January 2021); the World Bank ISR records 49,000 beneficiary households as of 15 October 2021 without saying how many had been paid.
NASSCO stood up an urban registry within months through USSD self-registration guided by the ML poverty map; over 1.75 million successful registrations (PAD, Nov 2021).
Material to many: 1,163 wards with over 20 million residents made eligible; PNAS simulation finds the ML maps would cut inclusion errors by 61.7% versus the survey-based benchmark.

ai_role.statement: Decisive at the geographic stage: the ML poverty map alone chose which 1,163 wards were eligible. Individual inclusion depended on USSD self-registration and in-person verification, not AI. Payment and registration counts come from World Bank operational documents, not from the map developers; the PNAS paper and World Bank blog are co-authored by the developers.
